newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Brief Taleban era leaves mark on northern city.
newsitem.headline: Brief Taleban era leaves mark on northern city.

text.p: The Taleban may have been driven from the opposition stronghold of Mazar-i-Sharif in northern Afghanistan, but traces of their radical vision of Islam remain.
On Monday, for the first time, some classes at Mazar-i-Sharif's Balkh University were segregated by sex.
And, foreign aid agencies in the city have been told to dispense with their Afghan women employees.

The Taleban took Mazar-i-Sharif two weeks ago after an opposition commander General Abdul Malik briefly defected to their ranks. Four days later they were driven out after street battles which cost them an estimated 300 dead and 700 captured.

During their brief tenure, the Taleban tried to impose their purist interpretation of Islamic law, banning women from education and the workplace and ordering men to grow beards. The Taleban have closed girls schools in all parts of Afghanistan they control, saying they would reopen them when they were able to make sure that education was fully segregated.
Balkh University closed during the Taleban takeover of Mazar-i-Sharif, but has since reopened.
"When normality returned, we received orders to reopen the university and to look for ways to segregate boys and girls," university vice chancellor Mohammad Mirza Paiman said.
"From today we have separated boys and girls," said English teacher Kanda (one name).
But that did not prevent Kanda, a 25-old-graduate of the university, from teaching an all-male class.
The previous leader of the anti-Taleban alliance, General Abdul Rashid Dostum, deposed by Malik, had run Mazar-i-Sharif on liberal lines, compared to the Ta;eban strictures.

When Malik forged his short-lived alliance with the Taleban on May 19, he agreed to impose Islamic Sharia law. Now a foe of the mainly ethnic Pashtun militia, the Uzbek leader said last week he still intended to enforce Sharia, but added that he did not agree with the Taleban's interpretation of it.

"We do not want the kind of society the Taleban want. We have our own Islamic religious scholars in the north who have approved women's rights to education and work. We will defend those rights," he told reporters.

"But we intend to stop corruption and other acts that are illegal in Islam such as gambling, theft, adultery and drinking," said Malik, who wore a turban and traditional baggy shirt and trousers in public while allied to the Taleban.
However, there were few signs that the northern leadership intended to pursue a Taleban-style drive for Islamic purity.
Beer was still available in the shops of Mazar-i-Sharif, even though the process of buying it has become more covert.
At the university, students said they wanted peace but feared what they might have to pay for it under the Taleban.

"When they arrived we were worried because the university closed down. They might be able to bring peace, but they would take away happiness," said Abdul Raouf, a 23-old-student in a class using handwritten English texts for want of books.
"We prefer women to have the same rights as us. Some of our best teachers are women," said another student.
